children: 0858 ET - The euro's recovery potential is likely to remain limited given an unresolved French budget crisis and high energy prices, ING's Chris Turner says in a note. While eurozone activity remains resilient, the European Central Bank's bank lending survey Tuesday showed tighter lending conditions and an unexpected fall in loan demand, he says. "It may be too early for the ECB to pour cold water on market tightening expectations at tomorrow's press conference, but the risks look to be building in that direction." The euro rises 0.1% to $1.1135 after reaching a 17-month low of $1.1111 earlier, LSEG data show. If the euro falls below support around $1.1065-$1.1110, a move towards $1.0880 is possible, Turner says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0848 ET - Bond markets trade sideways ahead of an expected interest rate hold by the Fed. Investors are mostly pricing in a hike in the following meeting, in December, but the outlook could change depending on today's communication. Inflation expectations remain above the Fed target and economic indicators have been robust. "Given the recent strength in US macro data, we think the Fed will lean very hawkish at today's meeting," TS Lombard's Daniel Von Ahlen says in a note. The 10-year yield is at 4.997%, slightly up from yesterday's settlement. The two-year also edges higher to 4.747% from 4.735%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

0837 ET - France's fiscal crisis could get worse before it gets better, but is unlikely to prompt action from the European Central Bank, Leo Barincou at Oxford Economics says in a note. A worsening bond selloff could be triggered by further protests, a government collapse over budget negotiations, further advancement of far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon or indications that the far-right's Marine Le Pen isn't serious about fiscal credibility. "Nevertheless, even a rise in spreads to 300bps wouldn't necessarily prompt substantial fiscal action, or ECB bond purchases," Barincou says. In this scenario, an outright crisis would likely be averted due to banks' limited exposure to domestic bonds and broader financial resilience, he says. "However, France would still face high economic and fiscal costs." (don.forbes@wsj.com)

0833 ET - The EU's plan to ban under 13s from accessing social media could help overcome the challenges that arise when individual member states come up with their own legal restrictions, Pasquale Stanzione, president of the Italian data protection authority, says at a parliamentary hearing on Wednesday. The comments come as several countries have moved ahead with their own rules for social media. Austria proposed a ban for children under 14, and Denmark is seeking to ban under 15s. (edith.hancock@wsj.com)

0832 ET - The U.K. government could leave out big policy announcements during this year's budget until the 2027 spending review, Omnis Investments' Patrick O'Donnell says in a note. The budget statement could be "a do-no-harm fiscal event, with a little increase in spending, a little increase in borrowing and a little increase taxation", O'Donnell says. Markets appear to already be pricing in a modest budget, raising the risk of a repricing if the Treasury Chief John Healey makes big unexpected policy changes, he says. Ten-year gilt yields fall 1.9 basis points to 5.322%, Tradeweb data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0827 ET - The Bank of Canada won't just decide on interest rates Wednesday, it also will release updated economic projections. Bank of Montreal's Benjamin Reitzes says this comes with an added wrinkle as the bank is using a new forecasting model, Prima. The economist says to expect the inflation forecast to be lifted, with 3% on the headline measure persisting into 2027 and potentially lingering above the central bank's 2% target into 2028. Core inflation projections could be little changed, with the BoC's anticipated rate increase a credible rationale to keep the forecast steady, Reitzes says. He believes 3Q GDP growth could get a small upgrade to as high as 2%, while 4Q may be introduced at about 1.5%. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

0757 ET - Markets are over 80% priced for a Bank of Canada rate increase and five of the country's six major banks forecast a hike, Scotiabank's Derek Holt notes. Yet in terms of bias, the economist considers at least three possible scenarios from the central bank. One is that BoC Governor Tiff Macklem is likely to be cagey and he loathes forward guidance, which may mean he is highly circumspect and noncommittal. Another option Holt sees is that Macklem balances trade and commodity shocks against each other while generally leaning on upside inflation risk in a mildly hawkish stance. But then Holt says it is possible Macklem could sound extremely hawkish, leaning into persistently high energy prices and the possibility consecutive rate increases may be required which would increase the market pricing for another rate rise in December and probably January. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

0754 ET - Investors in U.K. government debt are hoping for a "no surprises" budget, AJ Bell's Dan Coatsworth says in a note. "A dull as dishwater budget is the best outcome for bond investors as they crave zero drama." Gilts have been relatively calm in the lead up to the budget, due around 1230 GMT, but yields could climb if investors aren't convinced about the government's commitment to fiscal discipline, Coatsworth says. Ten-year gilt yields are up 0.8 basis point to last trade at 5.348%, Tradeweb data show, tracking their eurozone and U.S. counterparts. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0735 ET - Eurizon favors a tactical long duration position, reflecting its more constructive view on European government bonds and the long end of the yield curve, Silvio Vergallo, head of euro government and inflation-linked bonds, says. "Higher starting yields and the growing impact of restrictive financing conditions support this stance, while flexibility remains important as economic data and market conditions evolve," he says in a note. Beyond duration itself, positioning along the yield curve is also important as certain maturity segments currently offer attractive income and roll-down potential, he says. "Selective positions aimed at a steeper or flatter yield curve make it possible to capture return opportunities without having to increase duration risk to the same extent." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0724 ET - Yields on European government bonds have risen significantly since 2022 and have returned to levels that more closely reflect economic growth and inflation expectations, following the prolonged period of low interest rates after the global financial crisis, Eurizon's Silvio Vergallo says in a note. "While current yields appear high compared with the past decade, they are by no means unusual from a longer-term perspective," the head of euro government and inflation-linked bonds says. What matters most for investors is the higher starting yield: European government bonds once again offer attractive income, providing a degree of protection against moderately rising yields, Vergallo says. If economic growth slows or monetary policy expectations shift, there is also potential for capital gains. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0723 ET - Nearly two-thirds of Canadian CEOs back Prime Minister Mark Carney's economic plan but hold serious reservations about officials' ability to quickly implement necessary measures, according to a new report from the Business Council of Canada. The council, which represents CEOs at blue-chip companies, says its findings are based on a survey of 100 members. "Our consultations revealed widespread anxiety about the capacity of governments to deliver," the council says in a report published ahead of the release of Canada's annual budget plan. "Fragmented responsibility, overlapping jurisdictions, slow decision-making, too much process and an institutional bias against [making] mistakes were among the reasons cited by members." Carney's agenda focuses on accelerated approvals for major infrastructure and energy projects to help reduce Canada's reliance on US trade for growth. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

0723 ET - U.K. government bonds and sterling are more likely to show a stronger negative reaction if Wednesday's U.K. budget disappoints than a positive reaction if fiscal measures are credible, Capital.com analyst Daniela Hathorn says in a note. "Sterling and gilts have remained relatively calm ahead of the announcement, suggesting markets are anticipating a cautious fiscal approach." A reassuring budget could ease gilt yields and support sterling but moves will be modest given relatively benign expectations are already priced in, she says. In contrast, disappointing fiscal projections could generate a disproportionate negative reaction, she says. Sterling falls 0.2% to $1.3274 while the euro rises 0.2% to 0.8377 pounds. Ten-year gilt yields rise 1.1 basis points to 5.352%, according to Tradeweb. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

title: Euro's Scope to Recover Looks Limited — Market Talk
